summary: Defines enhancements to the OSPF routing protocol so it can work efficiently over demand circuits, such as dial-up or pay-per-use links, which would otherwise be kept busy or brought up by routine OSPF traffic. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If you pay every time you make a phone call, you don't want to call just to say nothing changed. This lets routers stay quiet on such links until something real happens.

questions: how does ospf work over demand circuits
what is ospf demand circuit support
what is the ospf donotage bit
how are ospf hellos suppressed on demand circuits
subtitle: How OSPF can stay quiet on dial-up and pay-per-use links so the connection can close when nothing needs to be sent.

tldr.problem: OSPF sends Hellos and refreshes its routing information on a timer, which forces a dial-up, ISDN or X.25 link to stay open and run up usage charges.
tldr.mechanism: Routers mark LSAs with a DoNotAge bit so they need no periodic refresh, flood only LSAs whose contents really changed, and the two ends of a point-to-point demand circuit agree to stop sending Hellos once their databases are synchronized.
tldr.outcome: The data-link connection can be closed whenever there is no application traffic. The cost is some robustness and the loss of the database checksum variables as a synchronization check. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 3883.

facts.label: DoNotAge value
facts.value: 0x8000, the high bit of the 16-bit LS age field

facts.label: Stale DoNotAge LSA flush
facts.value: After MaxAge seconds in the database and originator unreachable for MaxAge seconds

facts.label: Link state header
facts.value: 20 bytes, excluded when checking for changes

today: RFC 1793 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 3883. The RFC itself states that its flooding change was to be included in future revisions of the base OSPF specification.

sections.title: The Demand Circuit Model
sections.content:
A demand circuit is a network segment whose cost depends on connect time, on usage (bytes or packets), or both. The RFC names ISDN circuits, X.25 SVCs and dial-up lines as examples. On such links a routing protocol should send as little as possible, and when the topology has not changed it should send nothing at all.

The model is simple. With no data to send, the data-link connection stays closed. When data appears, whether routing traffic or application data, the router tries to open the connection, sends the data, and closes the connection again after a period with nothing to send. OSPF itself assumes the circuit is available unless it has information to the contrary, such as a discouraging diagnostic code after a failed call. This is the "Presumption of Reachability" taken from the RIP demand circuit work.

A router is oversubscribed when it cannot open all its demand circuits at once, for example a router with one basic rate ISDN interface can open no more than two connections. Datagrams for a connection that cannot be opened are discarded rather than queued, and OSPF does not report this as unreachability.
sections.eli5: It is like a phone you only pick up when you have something to say. If nobody has news, the line stays hung up, and everyone just assumes the other side is still there.

sections.title: The DC-bit and the DoNotAge Bit
sections.content:
Two small changes affect every OSPF router that supports this memo. First, a new DC-bit is added to the OSPF Options field. A router sets it in every LSA it originates, which tells the rest of the domain that the router can correctly process DoNotAge LSAs. The only exception is an indication-LSA, which always has the DC-bit clear.

Second, the high bit of the 16-bit LS age field becomes the DoNotAge bit, equal to hexadecimal 0x8000. An LSA with that bit set is not aged while it sits in the link state database, so it does not need to be refreshed every LSRefreshInterval. The RFC writes such ages as DoNotAge+x. When two LSA instances are compared, the DoNotAge bit is masked off first, so an age of 1 and an age of DoNotAge+1 are treated as equal.

InfTransDelay is still added to the LS age when an LSA is flooded, even with DoNotAge set, and the age may not exceed DoNotAge+MaxAge. If it reaches that value the LSA is flushed, which keeps the protection against flooding loops. A router's own LSAs must never have DoNotAge set in its own database, so they are still refreshed every LSRefreshInterval, and that refresh repairs any copy elsewhere where the bit was set by a memory error.

Because DoNotAge LSAs never age, they could outlive their originator. A router must therefore flush a DoNotAge LSA when both of these hold: it has been in the database for at least MaxAge seconds, and its originator has been unreachable for at least MaxAge seconds.
sections.eli5: Normally every note on the notice board is thrown away after a while unless its owner rewrites it. A DoNotAge sticker says "leave this one up until told otherwise", so nobody has to keep rewriting it.

sections.title: Working With Unmodified Routers
sections.content:
An unmodified OSPF router probably treats a DoNotAge LSA as if its age were MaxAge. At worst this causes endless retransmissions: the old router acknowledges what it sees as a different instance, so the sender keeps resending.

To avoid this, DoNotAge LSAs are allowed in an area if and only if every LSA in that area's link state database has the DC-bit set. If any LSA has the DC-bit clear, a router flushes all DoNotAge LSAs from the area, and their originators reissue them with DoNotAge clear. This is an exception to the usual rule that a router flushes only its own LSAs.

For regular areas (not stub areas or NSSAs) the rule is widened to the whole domain. Area border routers announce DoNotAge-incapable routers across area boundaries using indication-LSAs. These are type-4 summary LSAs that name the area border router itself, with cost set to LSInfinity and the DC-bit clear. The RFC also gives guidelines for limiting how many are originated: a router with a lower Router ID than another router that already originated one into the same area should not originate its own.
sections.eli5: If one old-fashioned friend in the group cannot read the "leave this up" stickers, everyone goes back to rewriting their notes the usual way until that friend gets an upgrade.

sections.title: Suppressing Hellos on Point-to-Point Links
sections.content:
Changes at the endpoints of a demand circuit are controlled by a new interface parameter, ospfIfDemand. The two ends need not agree on whether a segment is a demand circuit, but for the full benefit on a point-to-point link both ends must agree to treat it as one. Configuring just one end is enough, because a router that receives a Hello with the DC-bit set treats the link as a demand circuit.

The agreement works through the DC-bit in Hello and Database Description packets. A router sets the bit in packets it sends out the demand interface. Receiving a Hello or Database Description with the bit set means agreement. Receiving a Hello with the bit clear that lists the router's own Router ID, or a Database Description with the bit clear, means the peer refuses, and the router goes back to normal periodic Hellos.

Once the neighbor reaches the Full state, Hellos stop, and the connection is assumed available until there is evidence otherwise. If the router decides the neighbor is gone, the neighbor goes back to Down and Hellos resume at the slower PollInterval. The InactivityTimer event has no effect on demand circuit neighbors in Loading or Full, and a connection closed just to save resources must not generate the LLDown event.

On broadcast and NBMA networks configured as demand circuits, Hello handling and the neighbor state machine are unchanged, because Designated Router election needs periodic Hellos. Those links still get reduced flooding but their connections effectively stay open.
sections.eli5: Two friends agree not to keep texting "still there?" once they have caught up. If either one says no, they go back to checking in regularly.

sections.title: Flooding Over Demand Circuits
sections.content:
Flooding is changed only when every router in the area has indicated DoNotAge support, that is, when all LSAs in the database have the DC-bit set. Otherwise flooding over the circuit is exactly as in the base specification.

When it applies, two rules govern what crosses a demand circuit. First, only truly changed LSAs are flooded over it. A new instance that differs only in sequence number and checksum is a periodic refresh and is not sent out demand circuits, though it is still flooded elsewhere. A change means a different Options field, either instance at MaxAge, a different length, or different contents after the 20-byte link state header.

Second, an LSA that is flooded over a demand circuit has DoNotAge set in the copy sent, unless its age equals MaxAge, so the router on the far side keeps it indefinitely. This also applies to LSAs sent in reply to Link State Requests and to retransmissions.

All routers also get one change to the flooding algorithm. If a received LSA is less recent than the database copy, the router normally replies by sending its own copy back, without acknowledging the older one and without placing its copy on the retransmission list. The exception is a copy at MaxAge with the maximum sequence number, in which case the received LSA is discarded. The RFC notes that the change helps on ordinary links too, since a stuck MaxAge instance can otherwise block a new instance from being flooded.

Virtual links are always treated as demand circuits by routers that support the memo. Point-to-MultiPoint interfaces negotiate Hello suppression separately on each component link, and negotiation may succeed on some and fail on others.
sections.eli5: The routers only ring the expensive phone when the news is really new. A "nothing has changed" reminder is kept to themselves.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The first example in the RFC has three routers, RTA, RTB and RTC, with one demand circuit between RTB and RTC. RTB is configured to treat the link as a demand circuit and RTC is not. The sequence runs as follows.

  • T0: RTB sends Hellos with the DC-bit set, and the two sides agree to suppress Hellos.
  • T1: The database exchange runs as on any point-to-point link, but LSAs sent over the circuit carry DoNotAge.
  • T2 and T3: Hellos stop, and after a period of inactivity the data-link connection is torn down. No LSA or routing table entry changes.
  • T4: RTA refreshes its router-LSA. RTB sees that only the sequence number changed and does not flood it over the circuit.
  • T5: RTA's LAN interface comes up, producing a changed router-LSA. It is flooded over the circuit, which has to be reopened.
  • T7: A file transfer between hosts reopens the connection.
  • T8: If the link is reported inoperative, RTB and RTC declare their interfaces down, send new router-LSAs and send Hellos at the PollInterval. RTC's old router-LSA is flushed if the circuit stays down for longer than MaxAge.

The second example shows a demand circuit in parallel with a leased line. A router that does not support the extensions joining the network, with its DC-bit clear, causes all DoNotAge LSAs to be flushed and flooding to revert to the normal behavior, although Hellos stay suppressed on the demand circuit. The third example shows an oversubscribed router that cannot open all three of its circuits, so a topology change may go unnoticed until a connection becomes free.
sections.eli5: The phone stays hung up through the quiet times, rings when real news arrives or someone needs to talk, and hangs up again afterwards.

sections.title: Costs, Topology Advice and Open Problems
sections.content:
The RFC lists what is lost. Periodic refresh normally protects against LSAs being lost or corrupted in a database, and over demand circuits that protection is removed, so the design depends on routers holding DoNotAge LSAs correctly. Also, the network management variables ospfExternLSACksumSum and ospfAreaLSACksumSum can no longer verify database synchronization, because the LS checksum covers the sequence number, which differs across demand circuits.

Topology changes are still flooded over demand circuits, so the RFC recommends putting demand circuits inside stub areas or NSSAs. This isolates them from external routing changes, which are often the most frequent. Isolated stub areas or NSSAs can also be converted independently, while regular areas must all be converted before the feature takes effect in them.

The oversubscription problem is left as future work. Even when a spanning tree of connections could serve all sources, one may not form, and routers see all demand circuits as equally available whether or not they are open. Delaying topology flooding until a circuit is opened for application traffic, either always or by configuration, is explicitly unsupported. The RFC says security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.eli5: Staying quiet saves money but means nobody double-checks the notes, and some tricky jobs, like running out of phone lines, are left for later.

items.title: DC-bit
items.text: A new Options bit saying the router can process DoNotAge LSAs.

items.title: DoNotAge
items.text: The high bit of the LS age field, 0x8000. The LSA is not aged.

items.title: ospfIfDemand
items.text: New interface parameter marking a demand circuit.

items.title: PollInterval
items.text: Slower Hello interval, now also used on point-to-point networks.
